episode_title: Fixed Ops Friday w/ Dave Rogers, Tully Williams, Ed Roberts, & Richard Lupo | Daily Dealer Live
question: Why are repair orders declining in automotive dealerships?
transcript_excerpt: There are two competing explanations: Theory one, there are fewer units in operation coming through because of lower vehicle sales in prior year. Theory two, dealers are losing customers because we create too much friction, can't get someone on the phone, can't get an appointment, bad online scheduling, inaccurate wait times. Richard estimates UIO at 35-40 percent of the decline, with the remaining 60-65 percent attributable to dealer self-inflicted failure through friction in the customer experience.

episode_title: Fixed Ops Friday w/ Dave Rogers, Tully Williams, Ed Roberts, & Richard Lupo | Daily Dealer Live
question: What role does customer friction play in repair order decline compared to market availability?
transcript_excerpt: Dave Rogers argues friction accounts for probably 50 percent of the issue, citing that dealers make it very difficult to do business through too many rules of engagement when customers call, poor phone availability, and an attitude of saying no first instead of yes. He emphasizes the need to say yes and find solutions like offering loaner vehicles rather than creating conditions that make customers hang up and go elsewhere.

episode_title: Fixed Ops Friday w/ Dave Rogers, Tully Williams, Ed Roberts, & Richard Lupo | Daily Dealer Live
question: How should dealership service departments answer incoming phone calls to improve customer retention?
transcript_excerpt: Richard Lupo advocates for proactive solutions, noting that Apple Tree Automotive uses an AI agent that catches every single call, logs it, and schedules approximately 30 percent of appointments through AI with successful transfers. However, Tully Williams counters that he wants to maintain human-to-human contact during business hours, reserving AI for after-hours options, stating the dealership has been in business for 105 years and customers prefer talking to people rather than robots.

episode_title: Fixed Ops Friday w/ Dave Rogers, Tully Williams, Ed Roberts, & Richard Lupo | Daily Dealer Live
question: What percentage of routine vehicle service will migrate to mobile service outside dealership locations?
transcript_excerpt: Ed Roberts predicted that within five years, 60 percent of service visits will be mobile. Richard Lupo estimates 50 percent of routine maintenance like oil changes and tire rotations will be done outside the brick-and-mortar facility within a few short years. Dave Rogers agrees that customers would accept this split, saying if dealers meet customers halfway on 50 percent of the work, customers will give them the other 50 percent.

episode_title: Fixed Ops Friday w/ Dave Rogers, Tully Williams, Ed Roberts, & Richard Lupo | Daily Dealer Live
question: Should dealerships prioritize gaining more customer demand or eliminating customer friction in service operations?
transcript_excerpt: Dave Rogers and Tully Williams both chose 20 percent more demand, with Tully noting he would turn increased demand into no friction anyway. Richard Lupo chose zero customer friction, arguing that if you create that experience, the business will build naturally. Sam Dark challenged Dave and Tully by asking why the market should give dealerships more customers if their current friction levels are leaking customers to the aftermarket.

episode_title: Fixed Ops Friday w/ Dave Rogers, Tully Williams, Ed Roberts, & Richard Lupo | Daily Dealer Live
question: How has OEM data sharing with parts suppliers impacted automotive parts availability in dealerships?
transcript_excerpt: The panel discovered a significant supply chain problem: OEMs are not supplying their part suppliers with visibility into sales data, forcing suppliers to anticipate demand without that critical information. Dave Rogers found it fascinating that companies have extensive data but don't aggregate it for usefulness, leaving suppliers unable to know parts availability. Tully Williams noted that parts suppliers are asking OEMs to simply give them the data so they can better anticipate part needs.

episode_title: Fixed Ops Friday w/ Dave Rogers, Tully Williams, Ed Roberts, & Richard Lupo | Daily Dealer Live
question: Should dealerships follow OEM-recommended maintenance intervals or adopt more frequent service schedules?
transcript_excerpt: Tully Williams was the sole dissenter on the panel, believing the factory should dictate maintenance intervals and dealerships should stay by those factory standards. The other three guests advocated for more advanced rotation schedules, such as oil changes every six months, whereas Tully's manufacturers predominantly recommend one-year intervals. Tully emphasized the importance of adhering to factory standards set by OEM engineers.
